newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees progress in opening Japanese wood market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees progress in opening Japanese wood market.

text.p: The United States is likely to drop Japan's wood-products industry from a trade watch list this month, a Clinton administration official said Thursday, citing progress made by exporters over the past two years.

Gordana Earp, deputy assistant trade representative, said the administration likely would agree with an industry recommendation to drop Japan from the so-called Super 301 watch list for wood products.

"We have seen that progress has been made, and we are satisfied the commitments have been made," she told reporters at an industry conference. "I believe we will most likely go along with the recommendation."
However, she said Japan likely would remain on the watch list for its barriers to U.S. paper manufacturers, who have only about a 1 percent share of the Japanese market despite a trade agreement.
The list, due to be published Sept. 30 by U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, puts countries on notice that their trade practices could draw draw retaliatory U.S. measures.

Based on commitments made by Japan, industry officials said they expected U.S. exports of value-added wood products such as lumber and plywood to rise 20 percent annually over the next five years from last year's level of about $1 billion.
Exports of raw logs, which have not been subject to Japanese barriers, are expected to remain steady at the current level of about $1.7 billion, officials said.
Rick Holley, chairman and chief executive officer of Plum Creek Timber Co., noted that Japan is the world's No. 1 housing market with 1.6 million projected housing starts this year.

"Greater access to this market means greater sales to U.S. wood products manufacturers," Holley said, speaking on behalf of the American Forest & Paper Association, the industry group that asked the administration to drop Japan from the list.
Holley added that sales of more profitable engineered wood and finished products account for a rising percentage of total exports.

Holley praised the Japanese government for changes including the approval of construction of three-story apartment buildings in suburban areas, acceptance of U.S. lumber grades and agreement to exchange technical data.

He said U.S. marketing efforts over the past decade had helped by winning consumer acceptance of American-style wood-frame construction rather than the traditional but more costly Japanese post-and-beam style.

Holley noted that the industry still faced tariffs on lumber, plywood and finished products, an issue expected to be raised in November, when trade ministers from Pacific Rim countries meet in Singapore.
